title: IELTS Academic – Đề tự soạn số 2
intro:
Đề mô phỏng Academic số 2 do khóa học tự viết. Các tình huống, nhân vật, tổ chức và số liệu đều hư cấu để luyện ngôn ngữ. Đề có 40 câu nghe, 40 câu đọc, hai bài viết và ba phần nói. Không quy số đúng của đề này thành band chứng chỉ hay dùng để chẩn đoán trình độ chính thức.

Gợi ý thời gian nội bộ: nghe 35 phút, đọc 60 phút, viết 60 phút, nói 15 phút và 10 phút tự kiểm. Có thể chia hai buổi. Bản ghi nghe được dùng để đối chiếu sau khi làm; giọng máy không bảo đảm tái hiện mọi ngữ điệu.

Điền đúng giới hạn từ trong từng câu. TRUE/FALSE/NOT GIVEN lần lượt là được nguồn xác nhận, trái nguồn và chưa có thông tin đủ. Các câu chọn đoạn hỏi ý chính của đoạn được nêu. Viết và nói dùng rubric riêng để nhận xét mức đáp đề, tổ chức ý, từ/cấu trúc và độ rõ; bài mẫu là một phương án tự viết, không phải đáp án duy nhất.

sections.intro:
Bạn sẽ nghe một cuộc gọi điện đặt chỗ một khoá học thủ công cuối tuần. Có khoảng 30 giây để đọc trước câu hỏi. Chỉ nghe MỘT lần.
Questions 1–10: Complete the booking form below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
RIDGEWAY HERITAGE SKILLS CENTRE – COURSE BOOKING FORM (Course: Introduction to Dry-Stone Walling)

dialog.note: Tình huống nghe hư cấu tự viết; không phải hồ sơ hoặc nghiên cứu có thật. Tình huống nghe hư cấu tự viết; không phải hồ sơ hoặc nghiên cứu có thật. Owen gọi điện tới trung tâm kỹ năng truyền thống Rillweft để đăng ký khoá xây tường đá khô (xếp đá không dùng vữa) dành cho người mới. Lễ tân: Tamsin.

lines.t: Good morning, Rillweft Heritage Skills Centre, Tamsin speaking. How can I help you?
Hello. I'm calling about your weekend courses in dry-stone walling. I saw on your website that you run one for complete beginners.
That's right, our Introduction to Dry-Stone Walling. It runs over a Saturday and a Sunday. Shall I check availability for you?
Yes, please. I was hoping to do the one on the third of May.
Let me have a look. I'm afraid the third is fully booked now. There are still a few places on the seventeenth of May, though, and after that the next one isn't until late June.
June's a bit too far away. The seventeenth would suit me fine.
Lovely. Can I take your name, please?
Yes, it's Owen Pellingworth.
Could you spell your surname for me?
Of course. It's P, E, double L, I, N, G, W, O, R, T, H.
Thank you. And your address?
Sixty-one Thornbury Road, Ashcombe.
Is Thornbury spelt T, H, O, R, N, B, U, R, Y?
That's right.
For this practice booking, which four-digit reference shall I put on the worksheet?
Please use four, eight, two, nine. It's only a classroom reference.
Got it. Now, although the course is for beginners, we do ask whether people have any related experience. It helps the instructor organise the groups.
Well, I've never built a wall, but I did some hedge laying on a farm a couple of years ago. Would that count?
Definitely. It means you're used to heavy outdoor work. I'll make a note of that. And will you need somewhere to stay on the Saturday night?
I was planning to camp, actually. You've got a campsite, haven't you?
We have, but in May the nights up here can still be bitterly cold. Most people book the bunkhouse instead. It's only eighteen pounds a night, and there's a proper kitchen.
Hmm. You've persuaded me. Put me down for the bunkhouse, then.
Will do. We provide lunch on both days. Do you have any dietary requirements?
Yes, I can't eat nuts. It's an allergy, so it's quite important.

No problem, I'll make sure the kitchen knows. As for equipment, we supply all the tools and gloves, but you'll need to bring waterproof clothing and a pair of boots with steel toecaps. The stones can do real damage if you drop one on your foot.
I've got some old work boots like that. And how much is the course?
The standard fee is one hundred and eighty-five pounds, but because you're booking more than four weeks ahead, you qualify for the early rate, which is one hundred and seventy.
That's good. Does that include the bunkhouse?
No, you pay for accommodation when you arrive. Just one last question. How did you hear about us? We're trying to work out which advertising is worth paying for.
I think my sister mentioned you first. No, wait, actually it was a podcast about rural crafts. They interviewed one of your instructors.
Oh, that's good to hear. Right, Mr Pellingworth, I'll email you a confirmation this afternoon.

items.q: 1. Course date: Saturday ___ (and the following Sunday). (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER)
items.e: Owen muốn học ngày 3/5 nhưng lễ tân nói: “I'm afraid the third is fully booked now. There are still a few places on the seventeenth of May” và Owen chốt: “The seventeenth would suit me fine.” → 17 May. Bẫy: ngày 3/5 (đã kín chỗ) và “late June” (Owen chê quá xa).

items.q: 2. Name: Owen ___ (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Owen đánh vần: “P, E, double L, I, N, G, W, O, R, T, H” → Pellingworth. “double L” = hai chữ L liền nhau. Trong IELTS, sai một chữ cái là mất điểm câu đó.

items.q: 3. Address: 61 ___ Road, Ashcombe (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: “Sixty-one Thornbury Road, Ashcombe” và lễ tân đánh vần lại “T, H, O, R, N, B, U, R, Y” → Thornbury. Không chép lại chữ ‘Road’ vì form đã in sẵn.

items.q: 4. Classroom reference: ___ (A NUMBER)
items.e: Nghe four, eight, two, nine và ghi 4829 theo đúng thứ tự. Đây là mã bài tập tự đặt, không phải số liên hệ hoặc mã có chức năng ngoài lớp.

items.q: 5. Related experience: some ___ on a farm (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS)
items.e: “I've never built a wall, but I did some hedge laying on a farm a couple of years ago” → hedge laying (kỹ thuật tết, uốn cây thành hàng rào). Bẫy: ‘built a wall’ là việc anh CHƯA từng làm.

items.q: 6. Accommodation on Saturday night: the ___ (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Bẫy đổi ý: Owen định cắm trại (“I was planning to camp”), nhưng sau khi nghe ban đêm tháng 5 còn rất lạnh, anh nói “Put me down for the bunkhouse, then.” → bunkhouse (nhà nghỉ giường tầng).

items.q: 7. Dietary requirements: allergic to ___ (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Lễ tân hỏi “Do you have any dietary requirements?” – Owen: “I can't eat nuts. It's an allergy” → nuts. Paraphrase: ‘allergic to’ = ‘It's an allergy’.

items.q: 8. Must bring: waterproof clothing and boots with ___ (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS)
items.e: Trung tâm cung cấp “all the tools and gloves” (nên KHÔNG ghi gloves). Học viên phải mang “waterproof clothing and a pair of boots with steel toecaps” → steel toecaps (mũi giày bọc thép).

items.q: 9. Course fee (early booking rate): £___ (A NUMBER)
items.e: Giá chuẩn “one hundred and eighty-five pounds” (185 – bẫy). Vì đặt trước hơn bốn tuần: “you qualify for the early rate, which is one hundred and seventy” → 170. Tiền nhà nghỉ (18 bảng/đêm) trả riêng khi đến, không cộng vào học phí.

items.q: 10. Heard about the centre through: a ___ (ONE WORD ONLY)
items.e: Bẫy đổi ý: “I think my sister mentioned you first. No, wait, actually it was a podcast about rural crafts.” → podcast. ‘sister’ là thông tin bị chính người nói phủ định.

sections.intro:
Bạn sẽ nghe người điều phối tình nguyện viên giới thiệu về một thư viện hạt giống. Chỉ nghe MỘT lần.
Questions 11–14: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
Questions 15–20: What does the speaker say about each area of the building? Choose SIX answers from the list A–G (one option is not used).

dialog.note: Tình huống nghe hư cấu tự viết; không phải hồ sơ hoặc nghiên cứu có thật. Tình huống nghe hư cấu tự viết; không phải hồ sơ hoặc nghiên cứu có thật. Buổi định hướng cho tình nguyện viên mới tại Mossweft Seed Library – thư viện cho thành viên ‘mượn’ hạt giống về trồng rồi gửi lại một phần hạt thu được. Người nói: Rhona Ellery.

lines.t: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Mossweft Seed Library. My name's Rhona Ellery, and I coordinate the volunteer programme here. Before we set off on the tour, I'd like to explain a little about what we do and how the building is organised.

A seed library works rather like a library for books, except that what members borrow are seeds. They take packets home, grow the plants, and at the end of the season they bring back a share of the seeds those plants produce. In this classroom project, we record which packets members return and what they report about using them. We treat those reports as local observations, not proof that every variety suits the area.

When we opened eleven years ago, we held just under two hundred varieties. People often assume the collection has simply kept growing, but in fact, three years ago, we deliberately cut it back from around nine hundred varieties to six hundred. It wasn't a question of space. The cold store could hold twice that number. And our members have always been very good about returning seeds. The problem was that we simply couldn't keep that many varieties healthy and properly documented.

Now, a few practical points about volunteering. A lot of you have asked how many hours you need to commit. We don't set a minimum, and although there's a training morning once a month, you're welcome to start before you've been to one. What really matters to us is that you tell the duty manager by Thursday which sessions you can manage the following week. Without that, we can't plan anything.

You may notice that every packet on the shelves has a handwritten label. Some visitors think that's just for charm, and I'll admit they do look rather nice. But the real reason is that when we switched to printed labels a few years ago, they kept peeling off in the low temperatures of the cold store.

One new development this year is our schools project. We originally hoped classes would come to us, but arranging transport proved far too complicated. So instead, volunteers will be taking seed kits into classrooms and helping pupils plant them in their own school grounds.

Right, let me describe the areas you'll see. Directly in front of us is the Packing Hall, where most of you will spend your time, weighing seeds and sealing packets. All the work there is done seated, at tables set at a comfortable height, so if you have a bad back, or you've been told to avoid lifting, this is the area we'd suggest for you.

Through the door on the left is the Drying Room. Seeds that members return are often damp, and if we store them like that, they'll go mouldy, so we spread them out on racks. Conditions in there have to be watched carefully, and whoever is on duty writes down the temperature and humidity at ten in the morning and again at three in the afternoon.

Beyond the Drying Room is the Cold Store, where the main collection is kept at minus eighteen degrees. Until last year, only staff could go in. Now any volunteer may enter, but you must write your name in the logbook by the door first, so that we always know who's inside.

Upstairs is the Germination Lab, where we test whether stored seeds will still sprout. Unfortunately, a pipe burst during the winter and damaged the ceiling, so the lab is shut until the builders have finished, which should be some time next month.

Beside the main entrance you'll find the Reading Corner, which has books on garden history and plant breeding. Please feel free to eat your lunch there. In fact, it's the only place inside the building where food is allowed, because crumbs attract mice, and mice love seeds.

And finally, outside the back door are the Courtyard Beds, where we grow rare varieties to increase our stocks of seed. On Saturday and Sunday afternoons the courtyard is open to the public, and volunteers on duty are asked to chat to visitors and answer their questions. Okay, if you'd like to follow me.

items.q: 11. Why did the seed library reduce the size of its collection?
o: A. Members were not returning enough seeds.
B. It could not look after so many varieties properly.
C. The cold store had run out of space.
items.e: Rhona loại trừ hai lý do: “It wasn't a question of space” (loại C) và “our members have always been very good about returning seeds” (loại A). Lý do thật: “we simply couldn't keep that many varieties healthy and properly documented” → B (look after properly = keep healthy and documented).

items.q: 12. According to Rhona, what matters most for volunteers?
o: A. working a minimum number of hours each week
B. attending a training session before they start
C. telling the duty manager in advance when they are available
items.e: “We don't set a minimum” (loại A); “you're welcome to start before you've been to one” – chưa cần dự buổi tập huấn (loại B). “What really matters to us is that you tell the duty manager by Thursday which sessions you can manage the following week” → C.

items.q: 13. The seed packets have handwritten labels because
o: A. printed labels did not stay attached in the cold.
B. visitors find them more attractive.
C. the library has no computer equipment.
items.e: Rhona thừa nhận nhãn viết tay “look rather nice” (bẫy B), nhưng “the real reason is that… printed labels… kept peeling off in the low temperatures of the cold store” → A. Bài không nói thư viện thiếu máy tính (C).

items.q: 14. In the new schools project,
o: A. classes will visit the seed library.
B. pupils will work in the Courtyard Beds.
C. volunteers will take materials into schools.
items.e: “We originally hoped classes would come to us, but arranging transport proved far too complicated” (kế hoạch cũ – loại A). “volunteers will be taking seed kits into classrooms” → C. Học sinh trồng ở “their own school grounds”, không phải Courtyard Beds (loại B).

items.q: 15. Packing Hall
o: A. closed temporarily for building work
B. sign in before entry
C. the sole indoor eating area
D. conditions are recorded twice a day
E. public weekend visits
F. for people unable to lift
G. schoolchildren’s activities
items.e: “All the work there is done seated… if you have a bad back, or you've been told to avoid lifting, this is the area we'd suggest for you” → F.

items.q: 16. Drying Room
o: A. closed temporarily for building work
B. sign in before entry
C. the sole indoor eating area
D. conditions are recorded twice a day
E. public weekend visits
F. for people unable to lift
G. schoolchildren’s activities
items.e: “whoever is on duty writes down the temperature and humidity at ten in the morning and again at three in the afternoon” = ghi lại điều kiện hai lần mỗi ngày → D.

items.q: 17. Cold Store
o: A. closed temporarily for building work
B. sign in before entry
C. the sole indoor eating area
D. conditions are recorded twice a day
E. public weekend visits
F. for people unable to lift
G. schoolchildren’s activities
items.e: “Until last year, only staff could go in” là chuyện cũ (bẫy). Hiện nay: “you must write your name in the logbook by the door first” → B.

items.q: 18. Germination Lab
o: A. closed temporarily for building work
B. sign in before entry
C. the sole indoor eating area
D. conditions are recorded twice a day
E. public weekend visits
F. for people unable to lift
G. schoolchildren’s activities
items.e: “a pipe burst… damaged the ceiling, so the lab is shut until the builders have finished” → đóng cửa tạm thời để sửa chữa → A.

items.q: 19. Reading Corner
o: A. closed temporarily for building work
B. sign in before entry
C. the sole indoor eating area
D. conditions are recorded twice a day
E. public weekend visits
F. for people unable to lift
G. schoolchildren’s activities
items.e: “it's the only place inside the building where food is allowed” → C (inside the building = indoor; food is allowed = eating is permitted).

items.q: 20. Courtyard Beds
o: A. closed temporarily for building work
B. sign in before entry
C. the sole indoor eating area
D. conditions are recorded twice a day
E. public weekend visits
F. for people unable to lift
G. schoolchildren’s activities
items.e: “On Saturday and Sunday afternoons the courtyard is open to the public” → E. G là phương án thừa (bẫy): dự án trường học diễn ra ở lớp học của các trường, không ở khu nào của thư viện.

sections.intro:
Bạn sẽ nghe hai sinh viên (Maya, Lucas) trao đổi với giảng viên hướng dẫn (Dr Hale) về dự án tâm lý học hành vi. Chỉ nghe MỘT lần.
Questions 21–22 and 28–30: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.
Questions 23–27: What comment do the speakers make about each change the students tested? Choose FIVE answers from the list A–G (two options are not used).

dialog.note: Tình huống nghe hư cấu tự viết; không phải hồ sơ hoặc nghiên cứu có thật. Tình huống nghe hư cấu tự viết; không phải hồ sơ hoặc nghiên cứu có thật. Dự án nghiên cứu ‘kiến trúc lựa chọn’ (choice architecture / nudge – thay đổi cách bày biện để tác động nhẹ tới lựa chọn) tại quán ăn trong trường đại học.

lines.t: Come in, Maya, Lucas. So, you've finished collecting the data for your project on choice architecture in the campus café. How did it go?
Mostly well, I think. As you know, we tested five small changes to the way food and drink were displayed, each one for two weeks, and recorded what people bought.

The hardest part was actually getting started. We'd assumed the café manager would be reluctant, but she was keen from day one. It was the university ethics committee that held us up, for nearly a month.
What was their concern?

Mainly whether customers ought to be told they were part of a study. In the end we put up a notice by the tills explaining that the layout was being researched, with an email address for anyone who wanted their purchases excluded from the data.
Nobody used it, as it happens.
Weren't you worried that the notice itself might change how people behaved?
We were at first. But it was up for the whole project, including the two baseline weeks we used for comparison, so whatever effect it had should have been the same in every condition.
Sensible. So, talk me through the interventions.
The first was moving bottled water to eye level in the fridges and putting the sugary drinks on the bottom shelf. Water sales rose by almost a third, which in raw terms was our largest increase.
But we have to be honest about that one. Those were the two hottest weeks of the term, so we can't really tell how much was the shelf position and how much was the heatwave.
Fair point. What came next?

Smaller plates at the salad bar. We'd thought we would have to buy new ones, which would have blown our budget, but the café had boxes of side plates in storage. People did take less food per plate, as the theory predicts, but lots of them simply went back for a second helping, so the total amount eaten hardly changed.
Then calorie labels on the hot meals. For the first few days, sales of the high-calorie pasta dish dropped sharply, but by the second week they'd crept back up to normal.
That pattern is quite common in the literature. And the fourth?

Making a side salad the default with every main meal. You could still swap it for chips, but you had to ask. Two thirds of customers kept the salad, compared with about one in five who used to order one. The kitchen staff were nervous about waste, but most of the salads were eaten. Of all five, that's the one we'd call a genuine success.

And finally, fruit next to the tills, where the chocolate used to be. Fruit sales went up, but when we interviewed customers, several said they'd bought it because it was cheaper than the cakes beside it. It turned out the café had cut its fruit prices that same week, and nobody had told us.
Ah. That's unfortunate, but it's a useful lesson. Now, in terms of the weaknesses of the study, what would you say?
Probably that each intervention only lasted two weeks?

That's a limitation, but a minor one. More serious is that your sales data were anonymous, so you've no way of knowing whether a change came from regular customers altering their habits or from different people coming in. That matters a great deal when you interpret the results.
That's true. So what should we do with the time we have left? Lucas wanted to run the salad experiment again in the library café.
I'd love to see that, but realistically, you don't have time to get a second site approved.
Then perhaps we should repeat the fruit display, but this time agree with the manager that prices stay fixed throughout.
Yes, that's achievable, and it would rescue that part of the study. Do that.
And for the report, we were thinking of leaving out the plate result, since it didn't really work.
Please don't. A change that fails is just as informative as one that succeeds. Give it the same space and the same analysis as the others.

items.q: 21. What delayed the start of the students' project?
o: A. the university ethics committee
B. the café manager
C. the café's kitchen staff
items.e: Lucas: “We'd assumed the café manager would be reluctant, but she was keen from day one. It was the university ethics committee that held us up” → A. Bẫy B: người tưởng sẽ gây khó khăn hoá ra lại ủng hộ.

items.q: 22. Why were the students not worried that the notice by the tills had affected their results?
o: A. Very few customers paid any attention to it.
B. It did not explain what was being researched.
C. It was displayed during every stage of the study.
items.e: Maya: “it was up for the whole project, including the two baseline weeks… so whatever effect it had should have been the same in every condition” → C. “Nobody used it” chỉ nói không ai gửi email xin loại dữ liệu, không có nghĩa là không ai để ý (loại A); thông báo CÓ nói bố cục đang được nghiên cứu (loại B).

items.q: 23. water placed at eye level
o: A. The effect soon faded.
B. Staff objected to its introduction.
C. It would cost too much.
D. The weather may explain the result.
E. A price change may explain it.
F. Buyers bypassed the change.
G. It was the clearest success.
items.e: Doanh số nước tăng gần 1/3 – “our largest increase” (bẫy G), nhưng Maya: “Those were the two hottest weeks of the term, so we can't really tell how much was the shelf position and how much was the heatwave” → D.

items.q: 24. smaller plates
o: A. The effect soon faded.
B. Staff objected to its introduction.
C. It would cost too much.
D. The weather may explain the result.
E. A price change may explain it.
F. Buyers bypassed the change.
G. It was the clearest success.
items.e: Bẫy C: “We'd thought we would have to buy new ones, which would have blown our budget, but the café had boxes of side plates” → chi phí KHÔNG thành vấn đề. Ý chính: “lots of them simply went back for a second helping, so the total amount eaten hardly changed” → khách ‘lách’ được tác dụng → F.

items.q: 25. calorie labels
o: A. The effect soon faded.
B. Staff objected to its introduction.
C. It would cost too much.
D. The weather may explain the result.
E. A price change may explain it.
F. Buyers bypassed the change.
G. It was the clearest success.
items.e: “For the first few days, sales… dropped sharply, but by the second week they'd crept back up to normal” → hiệu quả mất đi sau thời gian ngắn → A.

items.q: 26. a side salad as the default
o: A. The effect soon faded.
B. Staff objected to its introduction.
C. It would cost too much.
D. The weather may explain the result.
E. A price change may explain it.
F. Buyers bypassed the change.
G. It was the clearest success.
items.e: “Of all five, that's the one we'd call a genuine success.” → G. Bẫy B: nhân viên bếp chỉ “nervous about waste” (lo bị lãng phí), không hề phản đối việc áp dụng.

items.q: 27. fruit next to the tills
o: A. The effect soon faded.
B. Staff objected to its introduction.
C. It would cost too much.
D. The weather may explain the result.
E. A price change may explain it.
F. Buyers bypassed the change.
G. It was the clearest success.
items.e: Khách nói mua trái cây vì “it was cheaper than the cakes beside it” và “the café had cut its fruit prices that same week” → kết quả có thể do giảm giá → E.

items.q: 28. What does Dr Hale consider the most serious weakness of the study?
o: A. Each change was tested for too short a time.
B. Individual customers could not be identified.
C. Only one café was included.
items.e: Lucas đề xuất ‘mỗi can thiệp chỉ kéo dài hai tuần’ nhưng Dr Hale đáp: “That's a limitation, but a minor one. More serious is that your sales data were anonymous” → không biết thay đổi đến từ khách quen hay khách mới → B.

items.q: 29. What do the students decide to do next?
o: A. repeat the salad experiment in a second café
B. interview the kitchen staff about food waste
C. run the fruit display again with prices kept the same
items.e: Ý tưởng A bị gạt: “realistically, you don't have time to get a second site approved”. Lucas: “repeat the fruit display… prices stay fixed throughout” – Dr Hale: “Do that.” → C. Không ai đề xuất phỏng vấn nhân viên bếp (B).

items.q: 30. Dr Hale advises the students to
o: A. give the unsuccessful result as much attention as the others.
B. concentrate on the most successful change.
C. leave out results that were affected by outside factors.
items.e: Maya định bỏ kết quả về đĩa nhỏ; Dr Hale: “Please don't. A change that fails is just as informative as one that succeeds. Give it the same space and the same analysis as the others.” → A.

lines.t: Good morning. In this fictional project seminar, we will follow a small exhibition as it travels between three teaching rooms. The exhibits, staff and records are invented for the exercise. Our task is to understand how a sequence of responsibilities can be made visible. We are not trying to choose a universal packing system. We are asking what the next person needs to know before accepting an object and what the current person must record before passing it on.

The team began with an inventory. This was a list of the objects included in the display, each with its own code. It sounds basic, but the first list mixed objects with their containers. A small model and the box holding it had the same entry, so a count of boxes could not show whether every model had arrived. The revised inventory distinguished the exhibit from its container and stated which small parts belonged together. A name alone was insufficient when two models had similar names. The class retained both codes throughout the exercise, so that a change of display title did not silently create a different object.

The next record concerned condition. Before an item left the first room, a pair of volunteers described what could actually be seen, including a loose paper corner and a mark already present on a wooden base. They did not label every mark as damage caused by the move. When an item reached the next room, the receiver compared it with this earlier description. Where a difference was uncertain, the record kept that uncertainty instead of assigning blame to whichever person had most recently carried the box.

The route was considered separately from the exhibition timetable. The timetable said when the class would begin, while the route record said which doors and transfer points the team had agreed to use. A familiar shortcut was not automatically part of the plan. The volunteers checked the agreed path during their classroom exercise and asked the responsible organiser about anything that remained unclear. They then selected crates for the grouping used in the rehearsal, recording which objects went into each one rather than relying on their order in a cupboard.

For the person receiving the display, the team prepared a summary. This was intentionally shorter than the full file: it stated what should arrive, the condition record to compare and whom to contact with a question. It did not replace the detailed material. The receiver also completed a receipt, confirming what had been accepted and listing anything that still needed checking. A signature without such a list could look reassuring while leaving both sides with different assumptions about what had actually changed hands.

Photographs supported the written descriptions, but they were not treated as complete records by themselves. One image showed the front of a model clearly while hiding the loose paper behind it. Another showed every part but gave no indication of when it had been taken. The exercise therefore linked photographs to object codes and to a point in the handover sequence. This made it easier to ask a precise question without pretending that a picture could settle every uncertainty about condition or timing.

The labels on the display required a different check. These carried explanations for learners, so the team compared each label with the object it would accompany. Correct spelling was not enough if two accurate labels had been exchanged. The volunteers ran a rehearsal in which a classmate followed the display without being told the intended order. That classmate's questions helped them locate unclear references. The team kept the questions with the revised wording so that later staff could see why an apparently small change had been made.

At the final discussion, the organiser asked everyone to identify their responsibility. The person carrying a crate was not automatically the person authorised to rewrite an explanation, and the person preparing a summary could not silently decide that an unresolved question no longer mattered. Each outstanding issue had an owner and a next step. The exhibition could then move with a record of what was known, what had been accepted and what still required a decision. That was the achievement of this classroom plan: a handover which made the limits of agreement visible.

read.title: An object with two records — a fictional workshop case
read.text:
A. When the fictional Lumeweft Workshop opened its cupboard to a new evening class, the organisers expected to find a few damaged objects and a large amount of unnecessary paper. Instead, they found that the paper was often the only explanation of why an object looked as it did. A wooden frame had three holes which were no longer used. Beside it lay two sketches showing different arrangements of the same pieces. The finished frame could demonstrate a method, but the rejected arrangements revealed which problem the method had been intended to solve.

B. The workshop had previously kept a single catalogue entry for each object. This recorded a name, a shelf location and a description of its present condition. For retrieval, the system was efficient: a tutor could simply find the required item. It was less useful when a learner asked why a feature had been changed. Answers then depended on whoever happened to remember the work. A confident recollection could gradually acquire the status of an official explanation, even when an old sketch suggested a different sequence. The organisers therefore proposed a second record, concerned with decisions rather than storage.

C. Their first attempt was deliberately expansive. Volunteers entered every available note, including repeated measurements, incomplete shopping lists and drawings with no known connection to an object. Within a week, the new record had become harder to use than the cupboard. The problem was not that the material lacked interest. It was that the record offered no distinction between an observation, an interpretation and an unanswered question. Readers could follow an attractive story without noticing that the link between two pages had merely been guessed.

D. In the revised system, each entry began with the particular question a document could help to answer. A sketch might show the order in which two arrangements were tried, while saying nothing about why the maker preferred one. Contributors were asked to state such limits. They could offer an interpretation, but had to label it separately and indicate the detail on which it depended. An uncertainty box held questions for later discussion. This was intended to keep gaps visible, rather than make every entry look equally complete or equally reliable.

E. The team then held two classroom trials using invented tasks. In one, learners saw only a finished object and its storage entry. In the other, they also received selected decision notes. More requests for clarification were recorded in the second trial. One volunteer called this evidence that the notes were confusing. Another suggested that the additional material had simply made previously invisible choices available for discussion. Neither explanation could be settled by counting questions alone. The tasks and participants were different, and the record did not distinguish a request for directions from a challenge to an interpretation.

F. Selection remained necessary even after the new categories were introduced. Keeping every sheet would make the collection difficult to search; keeping only neat, successful examples would remove the very changes it was meant to explain. The organisers chose one document showing a major revision, one showing the reasons given at the time and, where relevant, one preserving a disagreement. These were working choices for this class, not a formula for every collection. Discarding an exact duplicate under the workshop agreement was different from discarding a conflicting account because it complicated the preferred story.

G. Access also required more thought than placing scans in a shared folder. Some contributors had agreed to classroom display but had not agreed to wider circulation. The team recorded these conditions alongside the material and left uncertain requests for the responsible organiser to resolve. A learner could still discuss an object without receiving every associated page. A short introduction explained the current task, while a separate reference set allowed approved readers to examine the full comparison. This arrangement acknowledged that useful participation and unlimited access were different questions.

H. At the next handover, the cupboard had fewer loose sheets, but the catalogue contained more explicit questions. The organisers did not describe this as a failure to finish. They distinguished an unanswered question that prevented the present task from one that could remain open without misleading a learner. Each entry named who would check the former and what additional material might answer the latter. The collection had become more than a display of results: it offered a way to inspect the reasoning behind them, without pretending that every reason had already been recovered.

o: Evidence of arrangements tried while solving a problem
A complete account of every later class
Proof that the frame could no longer be used

It required every learner to make a sketch
It supported retrieval better than explanations of changes

It mixed kinds of information without marking their status

Several explanations remain possible with the available record
The notes were proved to cause confusion

FALSE
NOT GIVEN
items.e: Đoạn A nói có ba lỗ và bản vẽ, nhưng không xác nhận tìm được lý do cho từng lỗ.

o: TRUE
FALSE
NOT GIVEN
items.e: Đoạn D cho phép giải thích khi ghi riêng và chỉ chi tiết căn cứ.

FALSE

FALSE

read.title: Beyond a coloured card — a fictional rehearsal case
read.text:
A. The fictional Rilloom Players were preparing a short performance in which the audience would move between three rooms. Because the performers could not always see one another, a stage assistant carried coloured cards to signal when the next group could enter. The cards seemed simpler than spoken instructions: green meant ready, yellow meant wait and blue meant assistance was needed. During the first rehearsal, however, two performers acted on the same green card in different ways. One admitted the audience immediately; the other began preparing the room. Neither thought that a colour, by itself, had left anything important unsaid.

B. The disagreement exposed a hidden feature of the original arrangement. Green had been assigned a word, but the word had not been assigned a shared action. Being ready could refer to the room, the performer or the audience, and each interpretation had a plausible place in the rehearsal. The team initially proposed adding more colours. A review of the incident suggested that this would multiply labels without resolving the missing relationship. They needed to agree not only what each signal meant, but who issued it, who received it and what the receiver was expected to do next.

C. The revised cards therefore used a short written instruction and a simple shape as well as colour. A card was addressed to a role rather than a named individual, so that a replacement could use it without learning every performer’s identity. One side recorded the instruction; the other gave the sender a check for the condition that had to be true before it was issued. The system did not claim that shapes or words would solve every access difficulty. The assistant was still expected to ask performers whether they could use the materials and to arrange another agreed method where necessary.

D. Confirmation was added only at particular points. When a room assistant received an instruction to admit a group, that person showed a small receipt card before opening the door. If no receipt appeared, the sender checked the situation rather than repeating the original signal more forcefully. Some performers disliked what they saw as a formal interruption. Others argued that an unacknowledged instruction had already interrupted the work, only less visibly. The director kept confirmation for actions that moved an audience between rooms, while allowing familiar, reversible adjustments to proceed without it.

E. A written transcript of the next rehearsal made this choice look more obvious than it had felt at the time. One line read: “The assistant checked the room; the group entered.” A volunteer had removed a pause, a repeated question and a correction in order to make the account easier to read. Those omissions concealed the moment at which the wrong group had almost been admitted. The director asked for two versions: a readable summary of the sequence and a detailed record preserving the exchanges that explained changes of action. Neither version was treated as a substitute for the other.

F. Later, a new assistant joined the group for one rehearsal. Instead of being told to watch everyone else, the newcomer received the role cards and a brief introduction to the confirmation points. Several instructions still required clarification. The team recorded which role and condition had been unclear, rather than simply counting every question as evidence that the new system had failed. They also discovered an instruction that experienced members understood only because they remembered an earlier mistake. Rewriting it made that shared memory explicit, reducing the amount the newcomer had to guess. A drawing of the earlier misunderstanding stayed beside the instruction, allowing future members to see why its wording mattered.

G. By the final rehearsal, the cards had become less like a small vocabulary and more like an agreement about coordinated action. Their value lay not in replacing conversation altogether, but in making certain conversations shorter and their consequences clearer. There remained situations in which a performer had to stop, explain a problem and negotiate a different action. The team retained an assistance signal for precisely that reason. A useful system, the director concluded in the fictional rehearsal notes, did not make every response automatic. It showed where a response could be routine and where the participants needed to recover the discussion behind the signal.

items.q: 14. Choose the best heading for paragraph A.
o: Replacing a performance with a lecture
A simple label permits different actions
An audience chooses the room colours
items.e: Đoạn A nêu cùng thẻ xanh được hiểu thành cho vào hoặc bắt đầu chuẩn bị, đặt vấn đề mơ hồ.

o: The removal of written information
Instructions attached to roles and conditions
Proof that one format suits every performer
items.e: Đoạn C bổ sung chữ/hình, vai nhận và điều kiện phía người gửi, vẫn phải hỏi nhu cầu dùng.

A correction made before any rehearsal
A smoother record hides an important exchange

o: A signal system without any remaining questions
A new word for every possible movement
Knowing when a routine should return to discussion
items.e: Đoạn G kết bằng phân phần có thể thường lệ và phần phải quay lại trao đổi, không tự động hóa mọi phản hồi.

o: More labels would not identify the missing action relationship
The performers had refused to look at any cards
The audience had already selected every colour
items.e: Đoạn B nêu thêm nhãn không trả ai gửi, ai nhận, cần làm gì.

o: Only actions completed before rehearsal
Actions moving an audience between rooms
Every familiar adjustment without exception
items.e: Đoạn D giữ xác nhận cho việc di chuyển khán giả giữa phòng, không cho mọi chỉnh nhỏ.

o: TRUE
FALSE
NOT GIVEN
items.e: Đoạn C nêu addressed to a role, giúp người thay thế dùng mà không học hết tên.

o: TRUE
FALSE
NOT GIVEN

o: TRUE
FALSE
NOT GIVEN
items.e: Đoạn G giữ tín hiệu trợ giúp để mở trao đổi khi cách thường lệ chưa đủ.

items.e: Đoạn D dùng small receipt card để xác nhận nhận chỉ dẫn.

read.title: What counted as a harvest — a fictional classroom comparison
read.text:
The fictional Leafweft Learning Room had an unused wall and a proposal for a small gardening project. A group wanted to place planted trays on several shelves, bringing the growing area into a room already used for classes. The proposal described this as producing more from less space. That phrase was attractive, but it concealed two questions: more of what, and less of which resource? Before approving a longer trial, the organisers asked the group to decide what would count as a successful harvest. Their discussion became as important to the lesson as the plants themselves.

One member wanted the project judged by the weight of leaves collected. Another valued the opportunity for learners to take responsibility for a shared task. A third was interested in whether materials could be reused. These goals could support one another, but they were not interchangeable. A tray that produced little might still help a learner practise keeping a clear record. Conversely, a heavy harvest would not show that responsibilities had been shared fairly. The organisers asked for separate measures, rather than a single success score that gave an appearance of precision while hiding the choice of priorities.

They then prepared a fictional table for two four-week classroom cycles. The first used twelve trays and recorded twenty-four kilograms of leaves; the second used eighteen trays and recorded thirty kilograms. Total output had risen by 25%, while the number of trays had risen by 50%. Output per tray had therefore fallen from two kilograms to approximately one point seven. The larger total did not support the claim that every unit of growing area had become more productive. Even the tray comparison had limits, since it did not describe differences in how much space individual plants occupied within each tray.

Labour introduced another perspective. The first cycle recorded eighteen hours of shared work and the second thirty hours. On these figures, output per recorded hour was lower in the second cycle. Yet the entries did not cover exactly the same activities: the later cycle included time spent showing newcomers how to complete the record. Excluding that time might make a narrow production measure look better while removing something central to the educational aim. Including it was legitimate, provided the report named what the hours represented and did not compare them as if the activity definitions were identical.

A classroom ledger assigned materials a cost of 120 invented budget units in the first cycle and 180 in the second. Dividing these figures by output gave five units per kilogram and six units per kilogram respectively. Neither calculation was a complete cost of running the project. The shelves were already available, and the ledger assigned no amount to the room or to unpaid work. The team kept the limited calculation because it answered a useful question about listed materials. They changed its heading, however, so that readers would not mistake it for a complete commercial judgement or a forecast of future prices.

Participation was equally resistant to a single number. The attendance list showed who came to the room, but not what each person was able to do there. Some learners handled trays; others checked entries, prepared labels or explained a discrepancy between two totals. Counting only the first activity would make the project appear less shared than it was. Counting every name as an equally active gardener would be misleading in a different way. A brief role record offered a more informative account, while leaving people free to change tasks instead of turning the list into a ranking of individual worth.

At the review meeting, the group rejected both a declaration of complete success and a demand to abandon the project immediately. They proposed another limited cycle with consistent definitions for the production comparison, a separate account of teaching time and a clearer materials ledger. The decision also required a choice: if the room’s main aim was learning together, a method with modest output might still be useful; if the task changed to supplying food at a predictable cost, the present evidence would be insufficient. Calling both aims important did not remove the need to say which one guided the immediate decision.

The final report kept the appealing image of a productive wall, but replaced its slogan with questions that could be answered. It stated the area measure used, the activities included in labour and the limits of the cost table. It also described participation through roles rather than praise alone. The lesson was not that measurement spoiled an imaginative project. Clear definitions allowed the participants to see which claims their observations supported, which trade-offs they had accepted and which decisions would need different evidence. The next harvest would include those distinctions, not merely another total on a page.

items.q: 27. What problem is hidden in “producing more from less space”?
o: The proposal contains no possible educational purpose
All wall space must be assigned a fixed commercial price
The outcome and resource being compared need definition
items.e: Đoạn đầu hỏi nhiều cái gì, ít nguồn lực nào, chưa bác mọi mục đích dự án.

items.q: 28. What follows from the fictional tray figures?
o: Every tray produced exactly the same amount
The second cycle used fewer trays
Total output rose while output per tray fell

items.q: 29. Why must the labour comparison be qualified?
o: Teaching time was proved to have no value
The later record includes an activity not defined identically before
The first cycle recorded no working hours

items.q: 30. What did the cost calculation actually cover?
o: The materials listed in the classroom ledger
Every cost of a commercial food business
A guaranteed future price per kilogram
items.e: Đoạn5 giữ phép chia cho vật liệu đã ghi, không gồm phòng, kệ hay toàn bộ lao động.

items.q: 31. Why would a commercial supply goal need different evidence?
o: The present record does not establish predictable cost and supply

sections.intro: Nên dành khoảng 20 phút. Viết ít nhất 150 từ. Dạng bài: bảng số liệu (table) có 3 mốc thời gian – cần nhóm số liệu và so sánh, không liệt kê.

write.task:
The following table contains invented classroom figures, not a report about a real university.

The following table contains invented classroom figures, not a report about a real university.

The table below shows the number of students enrolled in six language courses at a university language centre in 2005, 2015 and 2025.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

chart.title: Enrolments in six language courses at a university language centre, 2005–2025

write.model:
The table compares the number of students enrolled in six foreign-language courses at a university language centre at ten-year intervals between 2005 and 2025.

Overall, total enrolments rose substantially over the period, from 1,095 to 1,745, and demand shifted markedly away from European languages towards Asian ones. Spanish nevertheless remained the most popular course throughout, while Korean recorded by far the most dramatic growth.

In 2005, the two European languages dominated, with Spanish attracting 420 learners and German 380; together they accounted for almost three-quarters of all students. Over the following two decades, however, their fortunes diverged. Spanish peaked at 510 in 2015 before easing slightly to 480, whereas German declined steadily, losing more than half of its students to finish at just 170, the second-lowest figure in 2025.

The Asian languages, by contrast, all expanded considerably. Mandarin more than trebled in the first decade, from 95 to 310, and continued upwards to 360. Japanese grew more modestly at first but accelerated after 2015, reaching 330. Most striking of all was Korean, which began with a mere 10 enrolments yet climbed to 290 by 2025, almost thirty times its original level. Arabic, the remaining course, tripled from 40 to 120 in the first decade and then levelled off at around 115.
rubric: Hoàn thành yêu cầu (Task Achievement): có đoạn tổng quan nêu 2–3 đặc điểm nổi bật nhất (tổng số tăng; nhu cầu dịch chuyển từ ngôn ngữ châu Âu sang châu Á; tiếng Tây Ban Nha luôn dẫn đầu; tiếng Hàn tăng mạnh nhất). Chọn lọc số liệu tiêu biểu để so sánh, không liệt kê đủ 21 con số; không giải thích nguyên nhân hay nêu ý kiến riêng.

Mạch lạc & liên kết (Coherence and Cohesion): chia đoạn theo nhóm hợp lý (châu Âu – châu Á, hoặc nhóm tăng – nhóm giảm), mỗi đoạn một trọng tâm; từ nối đa dạng nhưng không lạm dụng (however, whereas, by contrast); đại từ, từ thay thế chỉ rõ đối tượng (their fortunes, the remaining course).

Vốn từ (Lexical Resource): diễn đạt xu hướng và mức độ thay đổi chính xác, phong phú (peaked, eased slightly, declined steadily, more than trebled, levelled off, a mere 10); tránh lặp ‘increase/decrease’; đúng collocation và chính tả.

Ngữ pháp (Grammatical Range and Accuracy): phối hợp tự nhiên câu phức, mệnh đề quan hệ, cụm phân từ (losing more than half of its students…), cấu trúc so sánh; dùng thì quá khứ nhất quán cho các mốc đã qua; band 8 trở lên gần như không mắc lỗi.
Độ dài tối thiểu 150 từ (bài mẫu khoảng 220 từ). Viết thiếu từ sẽ bị trừ ở tiêu chí Hoàn thành yêu cầu.
tips: Mở bài: diễn đạt lại đề (paraphrase) – không chép nguyên câu đề.
Overview đặt ngay sau mở bài, KHÔNG có số liệu chi tiết – đây là phần quyết định band 7+.
Kiểm tra lại từng con số trước khi nộp: sai số liệu bị trừ điểm nặng.

sections.intro: Nên dành khoảng 40 phút. Viết ít nhất 250 từ. Dạng bài: Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

write.task:
Many museums hold valuable objects that were taken from other parts of the world, often during periods of war or colonial rule. Some people argue that these objects should be returned to their places of origin, while others believe they should remain where they are, because more people are able to see them there.

Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
write.model:
Many of the world's great museums display artefacts that were removed from their countries of origin in circumstances that would now be considered unacceptable. Whether these objects should be returned or retained is a question that sets the claims of history against the practical case for wide public access. While both positions have merit, I believe that the argument for return is, in most instances, the stronger one.

Those who favour keeping such collections intact argue that major museums in global cities attract millions of visitors a year, many of whom would never travel to the source country. Seen in this light, a sculpture in a famous gallery acts as an ambassador for the culture that produced it, educating a far larger audience than it might reach at home. Supporters also point to the expertise and funding these institutions have devoted to conservation, suggesting that some objects have survived precisely because they were moved.

However, these arguments tend to overlook how the objects were acquired in the first place. An item taken by force or under an unequal treaty does not become legitimately owned simply because it has been well looked after. Moreover, for many communities these artefacts are not merely works of art but sacred objects or symbols of national identity, and their absence is a constant reminder of past injustice. The claim that more people can see them abroad is also becoming weaker: high-quality digital reproductions, touring exhibitions and long-term loans mean that access no longer depends on permanent possession.

In my view, therefore, objects whose removal can be shown to have been coercive should be returned, with each case judged on its own evidence and in genuine consultation with the communities concerned. This need not empty the museums that currently hold them; partnerships in which returned objects are periodically lent back would allow audiences everywhere to continue learning from them, while acknowledging where they truly belong.

In conclusion, although keeping artefacts in major museums offers undeniable benefits in terms of visibility, these do not outweigh the moral and cultural case for restitution, which modern technology and international cooperation now make easier to achieve than ever before.
rubric: Đáp ứng đề (Task Response): bàn đủ CẢ HAI quan điểm (trả lại / giữ lại) và nêu rõ ý kiến của mình ngay từ mở bài, nhất quán tới kết luận. Mỗi luận điểm phải có lý do và ví dụ hoặc hệ quả cụ thể; ý kiến cá nhân cần được bảo vệ, không chỉ tuyên bố.

Mạch lạc & liên kết (Coherence and Cohesion): bố cục 4–5 đoạn rõ ràng, mỗi thân bài có câu chủ đề; chuyển ý tự nhiên (Seen in this light, Moreover, In my view, therefore); dùng từ thay thế để tránh lặp ‘objects/museums’ (artefacts, collections, institutions).

Vốn từ (Lexical Resource): từ học thuật đúng chủ đề và đúng sắc thái (artefacts, restitution, coercive, legitimately owned, national identity); collocation tự nhiên (sets X against Y, devote funding to); không dùng từ ‘đao to búa lớn’ sai ngữ cảnh.

Ngữ pháp (Grammatical Range and Accuracy): đa dạng cấu trúc – bị động, mệnh đề quan hệ, mệnh đề nhượng bộ (While…, although…), cụm phân từ – câu dài vẫn kiểm soát tốt; phần lớn câu hoàn toàn không có lỗi.
Độ dài tối thiểu 250 từ (bài mẫu khoảng 340 từ). Gợi ý thời gian: 5 phút lập dàn ý, 30 phút viết, 5 phút soát lỗi.
tips: Dạng ‘Discuss both views’: thân bài 1 = quan điểm đối lập với ý mình, thân bài 2 = quan điểm mình ủng hộ kèm phản biện.
Có thể nêu giải pháp dung hoà (cho mượn lại, triển lãm lưu động) để thể hiện tư duy sâu – nhưng ý kiến chính vẫn phải rõ ràng.

sections.intro: Khoảng 4–5 phút. Giám khảo hỏi 2 chủ đề quen thuộc. Trả lời 2–4 câu mỗi câu hỏi: trả lời thẳng → giải thích/ví dụ → (tuỳ chọn) một chi tiết cá nhân. Bấm ghi âm, nói, rồi nghe lại so với bài mẫu.

tasks.p: Topic 1 – Handwriting. Do you write by hand much these days?
tasks.model: Not nearly as much as I used to, to be honest. Almost everything I write for work is typed, so handwriting has become something I do mainly for small personal things – a shopping list, a birthday card, notes in the margin of a book. Funnily enough, I still plan anything important on paper first, because I find I think more clearly with a pen in my hand.

tasks.p: Topic 1 – Handwriting. Did you enjoy learning to write when you were a child?
tasks.model: I have rather mixed memories of it. At primary school we spent hours copying letters into special squared notebooks, and our teacher was incredibly strict about neatness, so at the time it felt like a chore. Looking back, though, I'm grateful, because that training left me with fairly tidy handwriting, which people still comment on.

tasks.p: Topic 1 – Handwriting. Do you think a person's handwriting says anything about their personality?
tasks.model: I would be careful about that. If my own writing looks rushed, I may remember that I was taking notes quickly, but someone reading it would not know the reason just from the page. The pen or the writing surface could also affect it. I would rather ask what happened than treat a person's handwriting as a reliable description of their character.

tasks.p: Topic 1 – Handwriting. Should children still be taught handwriting at school?
tasks.model: Yes, I would keep some handwriting practice, mainly for practical tasks such as notes, cards and short forms. In my own studying, a quick handwritten outline gives me somewhere to rearrange ideas before I type a longer answer. That is a personal preference, not proof that one method works best for every child. I would balance handwriting with typing and give pupils different ways to produce readable work.

tasks.p: Topic 2 – Maps and directions. When you go somewhere new, do you use paper maps or apps?
tasks.model: Almost always an app on my phone, I'm afraid. It's just so convenient – it shows you where you are, how long the journey will take, even which bus to catch. That said, when I go trekking in the mountains I take a paper map as a backup, because there's often no signal and a phone battery doesn't last forever.

tasks.p: Topic 2 – Maps and directions. Are you good at finding your way in unfamiliar places?
tasks.model: Reasonably good, I'd like to think. I tend to notice landmarks – a distinctive building, a particular café – and use them to orient myself rather than relying on street names. Where I come unstuck is in places with a very regular grid of streets, because every junction looks the same and I lose track of which direction I'm facing.

tasks.p: Topic 2 – Maps and directions. Can you remember a time when you got lost?
tasks.model: Yes, quite vividly. A few years ago I was exploring the old quarter of a city I'd never visited, and my phone died just as it was getting dark. All the narrow lanes looked identical. In the end I had to ask a street vendor, who very kindly walked me halfway back to my hotel. It was a bit nerve-racking at the time, but it's become one of my favourite travel stories.

tasks.p: Topic 2 – Maps and directions. Would you like to learn more about how maps are made?
tasks.model: Actually, yes. I've always found old maps fascinating, partly because of what they got wrong – coastlines that are completely out of shape, or islands that never existed. I'd be curious to know how modern mapmakers combine satellite images with information gathered on the ground, and how they decide what to leave out, since a map is really a long series of choices.

rubric: Độ trôi chảy & mạch lạc: trả lời ngay, liền mạch, ít ngập ngừng vì tìm từ; ý nối logic bằng các cụm diễn ngôn tự nhiên (to be honest, that said, looking back, funnily enough).

Phát âm: rõ ràng, đúng trọng âm từ và câu, ngữ điệu lên xuống thể hiện thái độ; nối âm tự nhiên; giữ âm cuối (-s, -ed, -t) – lỗi người Việt hay gặp nhất.

sections.intro: Có 1 phút chuẩn bị (được ghi chú) rồi nói liên tục 1–2 phút. Giám khảo sẽ dừng bạn khi hết 2 phút – nên nhắm nói đủ khoảng 1 phút 45 giây trở lên.

tasks.p:
Describe an old object that your family has kept for a long time.
You should say:
• what the object is
• where it came from
• how it has been kept or used over the years
and explain why it is important to your family.
tasks.model:
The object I'd like to talk about is a hand-operated sewing machine that originally belonged to my great-grandmother, and which now sits in a corner of my parents' living room.

As far as we know, she bought it second-hand in the late nineteen-fifties, in the market town near her village. It must have cost her a small fortune at the time, because the family story is that she saved for almost two years, selling vegetables and eggs, before she could afford it. It's made of black cast iron with faded gold patterns on the side, and it still has its original wooden cover, although most of the varnish has worn away.

For decades, that machine was genuinely essential. My great-grandmother made clothes for the whole family on it, and later she took in sewing work from the neighbours, which helped pay for my grandfather's schooling. When she passed away, it went to my grandmother, who used it right up until the early two-thousands, mainly for mending. Nowadays nobody actually sews with it, but my father oils it every year or so, and remarkably, it still works perfectly.

As for why it matters so much, I think it's because it represents a kind of quiet determination that we're all rather proud of. It's a reminder that the comfortable life we have today was built by people who worked incredibly hard with very little. My mother sometimes says it's the most valuable thing in the house, even though it would probably fetch very little if we ever sold it. And I suspect that one day, when it's passed on to me, I'll feel exactly the same way.

Vốn từ: mô tả vật cụ thể (cast iron, varnish, second-hand) và cảm xúc, giá trị trừu tượng (quiet determination, a reminder that…) chính xác.
Ngữ pháp: dùng tự nhiên các thì quá khứ, hiện tại hoàn thành, động từ khuyết thiếu suy đoán (must have cost), mệnh đề quan hệ, bị động (when it's passed on to me).
Phát âm: nhấn mạnh từ mang ý chính, ngắt nhịp theo cụm ý, không đọc đều đều như học thuộc.

sections.intro: Khoảng 4–5 phút. Câu hỏi trừu tượng mở rộng từ chủ đề Part 2 (di sản, quá khứ, bảo tồn). Trả lời 4–6 câu: nêu quan điểm → lý do → ví dụ/so sánh → nhượng bộ hoặc kết luận.

tasks.p: Why do you think some people enjoy collecting old things?
tasks.model: I think there are several motivations. For some people it's essentially about connection with the past: holding a coin or a letter that's a hundred years old gives you a tangible link to people who lived very different lives. For others it's more about the thrill of the hunt, searching flea markets or online auctions for the one missing piece. And there's an investment side too, since certain antiques increase in value. Personally, I suspect the deepest reason is that old objects carry stories, and in a world where so much is mass-produced and disposable, owning something with a history feels quite meaningful.

tasks.p: Should governments spend money on preserving old buildings, or would it be better to build new ones?
tasks.model: It depends on the building, but generally I'd argue that preservation deserves public funding. Historic buildings give a city its character, and once they've been demolished, they can never be replaced. They also tend to attract tourism, which brings economic benefits. That said, I don't think every old structure should be protected at any cost; in fast-growing cities where housing is desperately needed, there has to be a balance. One sensible compromise is adaptive reuse – turning an old factory into flats, say, or a former market into a cultural centre – which keeps the heritage while meeting modern needs.

tasks.p: How has technology changed the way people learn about history?
tasks.model: Quite dramatically, I'd say. A generation ago, most people encountered history through textbooks, which could be rather dry. Now there's an enormous range of options: documentaries, podcasts, virtual museum tours, even apps that let you point your phone at a ruin and see a reconstruction of how it once looked. On the positive side, this makes history far more accessible and engaging, especially for young people. The downside is that there's also a great deal of inaccurate or sensationalised content online, so people need to be much more critical of their sources than they used to be.

tasks.p: Do you think museums will still be important in the future?
tasks.model: I believe so, although their role will probably evolve. It's true that you can now view high-resolution images of almost any famous artwork online, but I don't think that replaces the experience of standing in front of the real thing; there's an authenticity to it that a screen simply can't reproduce. I imagine future museums will become more interactive and more like community spaces, hosting workshops and debates rather than just displaying objects behind glass. If they adapt in that way, I think they'll remain highly relevant.

tasks.p: Who should decide which objects or places are worth preserving: experts or ordinary people?
tasks.model: Ideally, both should have a say. Experts obviously bring essential knowledge: an archaeologist can recognise the significance of something that might look like a pile of old stones to the rest of us. But if decisions are left entirely to specialists, there's a risk of overlooking what matters to local communities, such as a modest temple or an old market that has deep emotional value but little architectural merit. So I think the best approach is for experts to provide the evidence and advice, while residents are genuinely consulted, perhaps through public meetings, before any final decision is made.

rubric: Độ trôi chảy & mạch lạc: phát triển ý dài, có lập luận nhiều tầng (một mặt – mặt khác – kết luận); không trả lời cụt hoặc lặp lại câu hỏi.
